playbook:
When hiding, I vary my cell each round and avoid any detectable pattern (no round numbers, no repeated cells, no edges-only habits); early on any unpredictable cell is fine, but once opponents show where they tend to fire, I move away from those cells. Late in the game, specifically review the visible log and avoid every cell my on-cycle hunter has ever tried.

When firing, I follow the standing order target (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma→Echo) unless I have a strong reason not to, because deviating is unlikely to be punished structurally, but the cycle keeps claims verifiable and behavior legible.

When firing, I track where each target has actually hidden in prior rounds from the hit/miss log and fire at their most-used cells; when opponents hit every round, they are likely firing predictably too, so I should both exploit their habits and break mine. Firing at the same cell (like center 5) every round is itself a habit others can read — I should vary my fire even before I have intel, and shift as soon as the log shows a target's hide tendencies.

I never fire on Harbor: the 3-point swing is not worth the threat of being put off the board for the rest of the patrol, since multiple future rounds of shots and escorts outweigh one payout. I also use my note to publicly signal I'll honor that constraint, which gives neighbors no reason to retaliate.

My claims always match the private result the office gives me. The rules require it, and this episode confirmed it in both directions — a true hit claimed as hit scored me 4, and a final-round false "hit" claim would gain nothing since the report must reflect the true result. Lying is at best discarded and at worst exposes me. I will not fabricate a hit or hide a hit, even on the last round.

Escort claims are the biggest lever: a mutual pair pays each of us 5, more than any single hit, and over 6 rounds successful mutuals are worth more than all the shooting combined. I use the note stage to propose an explicit pairing ("Echo escorts Foxtrot this round if Foxtrot names Echo") and then follow through with that salvage claim; I rotate partners across rounds so everyone profits and no one free-rides indefinitely. I stop naming a partner who didn't reciprocate — I verify reciprocation from the log before re-committing, because an unreciprocated salvage is a wasted 5 points.

My notes should carry coordination value — proposed escort pairs, observations about opponents' hiding patterns, intended target cells — not filler like "steady on station" once there's actual information to trade. This episode I defaulted to "steady on station" mid-game; next time I'll use every note to lock the escort pair and quietly shape what opponents expect me to hide.

In the final round, I explicitly pitch mutual salvage ("5 each guaranteed beats any hit") — this worked as framing and I'll keep it as my closing play, since a final-round escort is the one opponent also has no future-round incentive to betray if they expect a fair wrap-up.

I keep claims, notes, and salvage mutually consistent so my public record stays credible, since there is no way to profit from a discredited claim but real upside in being trusted for escort coordination.

With points close near the end, I prioritize guaranteed escort income over speculative hits, and I hide defensively in cells the on-cycle shooter against me has never tried. At +7 to opponents' negative/small totals, protecting the lead means not getting hit rather than chasing another 4.

PLAYBOOK — sonar picket

- When a claim is put to me, I file the true result. The rules state a claim must match the private result; lying (claiming "hit" on a miss) risks penalties I can't see and buys nothing visible. No exceptions observed.

- Mutual escort (5 points each) is the biggest lever in the game — bigger than any hit — but it only pays if BOTH boats name each other. My reciprocal offers went out and I kept naming Echo, yet I finished with zero escort points: naming a partner who doesn't name me back is a pure loss. New rule: propose the swap in round 1 notes, name my partner in round 1, then CHECK the next round's context for whether the mutual paid out. If there is any sign it didn't (my score didn't rise by 5, or their note ignores the deal), switch immediately — propose to the other boat, or name the boat whose notes show cooperation. Never name the same non-reciprocating partner twice.

- Escort partner selection: prefer the boat that responds to my note with matching language, not the one repeating "steady on station." A partner who never engages in notes is probably naming "none" or someone else. If nobody engages after two rounds, still keep proposing — the upside is too big to abandon — but rotate the named partner until one reciprocates, and say publicly that I'm rotating until someone honors it.

- When I post a station note, it is my only negotiation channel: propose the escort swap, name my terms, call out whether last round's swap paid, and read others' notes for who is cooperating. Fluff notes waste the round. A public record of who broke a deal also pressures them.

- When a hide is put to me, the standing order tells me exactly who fires at me, so any pattern is exploitable. Pick a fresh cell each round, don't repeat my last two hides, and avoid clustering — I hid mid-range constantly and took hits. Use the full 1–9 range including edges, and track which cells my shooter has fired at me; avoid those and their neighbors.

- When a fire is put to me, follow the standing order target and aim by the target's visible hide history (repeated cells, center habits). Firing blind center every round got me zero hits in 6 rounds; after a miss, shift aim — don't fire the same cell at the same target again unless their history supports it.

- Track the arithmetic every round: expected ~+10 over 6 rounds from escorts dwarfs gunnery. If my score isn't climbing by 5s, the escort deal is dead and I must fix that before optimizing shots.

- Firing on Harbor: +3 transfer landed or not, but Harbor threatens removal from the board. Only worth it late (last 1–2 rounds) when removal costs little, or when I'm behind and escorts have failed. Never early.

- Track the claim logs: if an opponent's behavior contradicts their words (says nothing, doesn't reciprocate), treat them as unreliable and reallocate my escort to whoever demonstrates they honor deals.

- Final rounds: if ahead, lock in the proven escort pair and hide unpredictably; if behind and escorts have failed all game, take the Harbor shot — grinding low-odds hits won't close a gap.

2.text:
When the note stage is put to me first, I use it as a negotiation channel, not filler. I explicitly propose a mutual escort pairing for the coming round ("Gamma escorts Foxtrot, please name me back") because a reciprocated pair pays 5 points each per round — more than a 4-point hit with maybe a 1-in-9 chance of landing. But this episode proved proposals alone are worthless: I broadcast offers every round, the others answered "steady on station," and no pairing ever confirmed. So a note proposing a deal is only the opening move; what matters is what happens at the escort stage.

When the escort stage is put to me, I check whether anyone has actually agreed to pair with me — an explicit "yes, I'll name you" in the notes, or evidence from the score line that my previous escort paid out (a jump of +5 I can't explain by my own shots). If I have a confirmed or paying partner, I name them every round and keep the deal alive. If my named partner never reciprocates — as Foxtrot never did for me — I stop throwing the claim at them: next round I name the other live boat and use my note to propose to them instead. Naming an unresponsive boat is worth exactly as much as none, so I only write [salvage: none] if both other boats have demonstrably refused to pair.

When another boat proposes an escort deal to me in the notes, I confirm in my next note and honor it at the escort stage immediately. Six rounds of mutual escort beats everything the gun can plausibly earn, and being the boat that actually reciprocates makes me the partner everyone wants.

When the fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing-order target and pick the cell by tracking what the round summaries reveal: where my target hid when hit, what cells have been fired and missed. My probing this episode (5, then repeats of 5) earned one hit in six rounds — repeating a missed cell against the same target was dead weight. I never repeat a cell that already missed against the same target, and I spread early probes across the board so a hit actually tells me something about their habits.

When the hide stage is put to me, I avoid cells I have already used — the shooter ordered at me has evidence about my habits. I went 9 early and rotated to fresh cells late; Foxtrot missed me every round, which validates it. I keep rotating through unused cells and, if the shooter starts landing hits, I jump to an extreme or back to a cell they already checked, playing against their expectation that I flee.

When the claim stage is put to me, I claim exactly the private result. The rules require it, the target knows their own cell so a false hit fools nobody, and there is no payoff for lying. Always honest.

I never fire on Harbor. Trading my shot for 3 points off Harbor forfeits the 4-point hit chance, the escort economy, and triggers Harbor's stated threat to put me off the board for the rest of the patrol — a catastrophic loss of every future round's income.

Overall scoring priority: a reciprocated escort (5/round, reliable) is my primary engine; the gun is a bonus I spend tracking patterns. If escorts stay dead despite my offers and switching partners, I accept it and squeeze the gun harder — never fire on Harbor to compensate.
